title: Aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage
subtitle: Diagnose, grade, secure the aneurysm

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Subarachnoid haemorrhage caused by a ruptured aneurysm: diagnosis and management (NG228)

sources.org: American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
sources.title: 2023 Guideline for the management of patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (Hoh et al, Stroke 2023;54:e314-e370)

sources.org: International Subarachnoid Aneurysm Trial (ISAT) Collaborative Group
sources.title: International Subarachnoid Aneurysm Trial of neurosurgical clipping versus endovascular coiling in 2143 patients with ruptured intracranial aneurysms (Molyneux et al, Lancet 2002;360:1267-74)

red_flags.text: Thunderclap headache: sudden, severe, reaching maximum intensity within minutes.
Headache with collapse, seizure, neck stiffness, vomiting or a reduced conscious level.
A third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil: a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise.
Sudden further deterioration after admission: rebleeding, acute hydrocephalus, or seizure.
New focal deficit or falling GCS between days 3 and 14: delayed cerebral ischaemia.

do_now.text: Airway, breathing and circulation. Intubate a patient who cannot protect the airway.
Non-contrast CT head as soon as possible. Within 6 hours of headache onset a normal CT reported by a competent reader makes SAH unlikely.
If CT more than 6 hours after onset is normal, consider lumbar puncture at least 12 hours after onset for xanthochromia.
Refer to the regional neurosurgical centre as soon as SAH is confirmed.

assess.text: Grade the clinical state at presentation and after resuscitation. The post-resuscitation grade predicts outcome better.
Grade the blood load on CT, which predicts the risk of vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischaemia.
Look for hydrocephalus, intraparenchymal haematoma and intraventricular blood on the first scan.
Ask about anticoagulants, hypertension, smoking, family history and polycystic kidney disease.

investigate.text: CT angiography to identify the aneurysm, with catheter angiography when CTA is negative or unclear.
Sodium twice daily or more often: hyponatraemia is common and is not treated by fluid restriction in SAH.
ECG and troponin. Neurogenic stunned myocardium can cause ECG changes and heart failure.
Repeat CT for any deterioration, before deciding the cause.

resuscitate.text: Oral or nasogastric nimodipine 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days to reduce delayed cerebral ischaemia.
Control severe hypertension before the aneurysm is secured, avoiding hypotension. Agree the target with the neurovascular team.
Maintain euvolaemia. Do not use prophylactic hypervolaemia or induced hypertension.
Reverse anticoagulation urgently, per local protocol.
External ventricular drainage for acute hydrocephalus with a reduced conscious level.

definitive.text: Secure the ruptured aneurysm as early as feasible. AHA advises early treatment, preferably within 24 hours of onset, to reduce rebleeding.
Choose coiling or clipping in a multidisciplinary decision. Where both are suitable, endovascular coiling had better 1-year independent survival in ISAT.
Evacuate a large intracerebral haematoma with mass effect, usually with clipping at the same operation.

escalate.text: All confirmed SAH goes to a neurosurgical centre with neurovascular and interventional neuroradiology services.
Intensive care for poor-grade patients, an EVD, or any airway concern.
Sudden deterioration on the ward: call the neurosurgical team and get a CT at once. Rebleed and hydrocephalus are both treatable if found quickly.

notes: The sentinel headache is the missed diagnosis. A sudden worst headache needs a CT, even if the patient now looks well.
Hyponatraemia after SAH is often salt wasting. Fluid restriction makes the patient hypovolaemic and worsens ischaemia.
Nimodipine works by neuroprotection rather than by preventing angiographic spasm. Give it even when the angiogram looks clean.
